summary: This work demonstrates quantum-controlled synthetic materials by entangling the lattice potential landscape of a superconducting Bose-Hubbard circuit with an ancilla qubit, enabling the system to evolve under superpositions of different lattice configurations. The approach generates novel strongly-correlated states where solid (Mott insulator) and fluid phases coexist as entangled $N00N$ states, which are probed and enhanced using many-body Ramsey interferometry and echo techniques.
motivation: Current analog simulators rely entirely on classical control of the Hamiltonian parameters. Interfacing analog many-body systems with small quantum computers would enable quantum-level control of synthetic matter, unlocking new capabilities for state preparation, characterization, and dynamical control of strongly-correlated states.
method: We implemented a chain of capacitively coupled transmon qubits ($J/2\pi \approx 9$ MHz, $U/2\pi \approx 240$ MHz) with site-resolved flux tuning to realize a 1D Bose-Hubbard model. An ancilla qubit controls transport by detuning the middle site by $U$, making particle tunneling resonant only if the ancilla is occupied. Superposing the ancilla state in $(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ creates a solid$+$fluid superposition, which adiabatic relocation in an inverted disorder potential maps to an entangled cat state.
result: For $N=5$ and $N=7$ qubits, we prepared multipartite $N00N$ states and verified entanglement through Ramsey fringes with fringe frequency shift scaling as $(N-1)\delta$ under perturbations. Using many-body echo with ancilla $\pi$ pulses, we suppressed dephasing from low-frequency flux noise, achieving coherence recovery from undetectable to visible oscillations in the 7-qubit case. Off-diagonal errors were measured at $\epsilon_X = (9.1 \pm 0.9)\%$ and $(17.7 \pm 1.3)\%$ for 5- and 7-qubit states respectively, with photon lifetime $T_1 \approx 45$ µs.
